explanation: Spores are produced in large numbers and are very small and lightweight, so they can be dispersed long distances by wind or water. They have thick, resistant walls that allow them to survive harsh conditions (drought, heat, cold). When conditions are favourable, spores germinate and grow into new organisms. This is seen in fungi, mosses, ferns, and some bacteria (endospores).

options.text: Spores combine genetic material from two parents
Spores are large and nutrient-rich for rapid germination
Spores are lightweight, resistant to harsh conditions, and can be dispersed widely
Spores can only grow in water

stem: What is the advantage of spore formation as a method of asexual reproduction?

explanation: The text specifically notes that microspores, megaspores, and spores of bryophytes/pteridophytes that give rise to a gametophyte are excluded from asexual reproduction because meiosis is generally involved in their formation, unlike true asexual spores (e.g. in Rhizopus or bacteria).

options.text: Because meiosis is generally involved in their formation
Because they never develop into new organisms

Because they require two parents

explanation: In epigeal germination (e.g. bean, Phaseolus), the hypocotyl elongates and curves, pulling the cotyledons above the soil surface. The cotyledons become green and photosynthesise briefly before withering. In hypogeal germination (e.g. pea, maize), the epicotyl elongates while the cotyledons stay below the soil surface. The cotyledons remain as a food source underground and do not photosynthesise.

options.text: Epigeal produces more seeds than hypogeal
In epigeal germination the cotyledons emerge above soil; in hypogeal they remain below
Epigeal only occurs in monocots; hypogeal only in dicots
Epigeal requires light; hypogeal requires darkness

stem: What is the difference between epigeal and hypogeal germination?

explanation: The text describes the haplo-diplontic lifecycle: a haploid gametophyte (gamete-producing) generation alternates with a diploid sporophyte (spore-producing) generation. In bryophytes the gametophyte dominates; in the rest of the plant kingdom the sporophyte dominates.

options.text: Gametophyte produces gametes and is haploid; sporophyte produces spores and is diploid, and they alternate
Both generations are diploid and produce gametes
The sporophyte is always the dominant generation in every plant group
The gametophyte only exists in flowering plants

Epicotyl is found only in dicots; hypocotyl only in monocots
